sources.title: The Rise of Competing Hawaiian States
sources.note: Academic synthesis of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century food surpluses, competing states, fragility, durability, and later island advantages.

sources.title: States without Archaeological Correlates? A Report from Hawaiʻi
sources.note: Peer-reviewed caution that no single archaeological event neatly marks Hawaiian state formation and that development was historically continuous.

sources.title: The Ancient Hawaiian State: Origins of a Political Society
sources.note: Academic book on the transformation from chiefly authority toward warrior kings and centralized island governments before European contact.

sources.title: The Prehistory of Hawaiʻi
sources.note: Academic overview of dispersed hamlets, wet and dry farming, ahupuaʻa, heiau, specialized production, chiefdoms, and state debate.

sources.title: Strategies for constructing religious authority in ancient Hawaiʻi
sources.note: Peer-reviewed archaeological sequence from fifteenth-century agricultural shrines toward later centralized priestly and political authority.

sources.title: Garden Offerings in the Kona Field System, Hawaiʻi Island
sources.note: Peer-reviewed dating of Kona farming and garden offerings beginning around 1400 with careful later political chronology.

sources.title: Household expansion linked to agricultural intensification during emergence of Hawaiian archaic states
sources.note: Peer-reviewed dates from Leeward Kohala households linking 1400 to 1800 residential expansion with agricultural intensification.

sources.title: A Fertile Landscape: Unearthing Agricultural Archeology at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes
sources.note: NPS archaeological account of fifteenth-century sweet potato cultivation, walls, dryland fields, and community field research.

sources.title: Kaloko-Honokōhau fishponds and fishtrap
sources.note: NPS evidence for long-used fishponds, circulation channels, dry-stacked seawalls, sluice gates, and careful marine resource management.

sources.title: Huilua Fishpond
sources.note: NPS account of Oʻahu aquafarming, a seven-acre pond and seawall, with an explicit uncertain construction date.

sources.title: Food, Subsistence, and Agriculture in Hawaiʻi
sources.note: NPS overview of canoe crops, fishing, wet and dry cultivation, irrigation, terraces, digging sticks, and erosion walls.

sources.title: Early Hawaiians at Haleakalā
sources.note: NPS overview of voyaging, introduced plants and animals, specialists, daily work, oral traditions, and island land divisions.

sources.title: Kauhale: Domestic Life of Nā Kuaʻāina
sources.note: Academic household archaeology from Kahikinui, Maui, including house clusters, earth ovens, prayers, cooking separation, and shared eating.

sources.title: Preservation of Nuʻu
sources.note: NPS survey of Maui agricultural terraces, house enclosures, shrines, toolmaking, burials, and radiocarbon evidence beginning by 1400 to 1600.

sources.title: Kahuku cultural landscape
sources.note: NPS place history for settlement and intensively managed mid-elevation fields by the mid-fifteenth century in Kaʻū.

sources.title: Kīpahulu Moku
sources.note: NPS archaeological interpretation of house foundations, reused walls, irrigated fields, fishing technology, and layered occupation.

sources.title: Archeology at Haleakalā
sources.note: NPS explanation of archaeology, Native Hawaiian terminology, surviving material culture, and the continuing significance of places.

sources.title: Discovering Haleakalā’s Past: Early Archeology
sources.note: NPS record of shelters, trails, quarrying, stone tools, survey limits, later replicas, and repatriation of disturbed burials.

sources.title: Kapa at Haleakalā
sources.note: NPS account of bark-cloth plants, soaking and beating, tools, watermarks, clothing, bedding, banners, and gendered craft history.

sources.title: Iʻe kuku and Kapa Making Workshop
sources.note: NPS and Native Hawaiian practitioner context for kapa fermentation, watermarks, pigments, clothing, bedding, ceremony, and living revival.

sources.title: Hawaiian Material Culture at Kalaupapa
sources.note: NPS museum and archaeological evidence for basalt tools, woodworking, canoe materials, surfing, sledding, kōnane, and ʻulu maika.

sources.title: Makahiki at Haleakalā
sources.note: NPS account of island variation, seasonal celebration, offerings, games, ritual movement, and the later evidence base.

sources.title: Aʻo: Educational Traditions
sources.note: University of Hawaiʻi curriculum grounded in Hawaiian educational traditions of listening, observing, practicing, family, and specialist learning.

sources.title: Ke Ao Mālamalama: Hawaiian family, childhood, and knowledge
sources.note: Native Hawaiian scholarship on ʻohana, collective responsibility, intergenerational teaching, oral history, and evidence from later records.

sources.title: From Oral Tradition to Written Word
sources.note: Hawaiian Mission Houses account of oral transmission and the 1822 first printed Hawaiian primer and missionary alphabet.

sources.title: First Hawaiian alphabet primer archive record
sources.note: Archive catalog record identifying the first page of the first Hawaiian book printed by Elisha Loomis in January 1822.

sources.title: Lāʻau Makamae o Hawaiʻi
sources.note: NPS guide to Polynesian-introduced and Indigenous plants used for food, lighting, dye, clothing, and medicinal purposes.

sources.title: Māla Lāʻau Lapaʻau Native Hawaiian Healing Garden
sources.note: University of Hawaiʻi medical-school garden created with cultural experts to sustain plant knowledge, teaching, and Native Hawaiian healing continuity.

sources.title: Water: Its meaning and management in pre-contact Hawaiʻi
sources.note: University of Hawaiʻi research integrating archaeology and Hawaiian traditions while emphasizing local water variation and change over time.

sources.title: Early Hawaiian Life on the Kalaupapa Peninsula
sources.note: NPS evidence for house sites, fields, irrigation, walls, temples, gathering, fishing, fresh water, forests, houses, and canoes.
